name: THE SNEAKIN' CELERY DOWN THE ALLEY BURGER (comes with bone marrow)

recipe.history:
Celery — Apium graveolens — is one of the most ancient cultivated vegetables, with evidence of its cultivation and use tracing back to the Mediterranean world of ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome. The Greeks and Romans knew wild celery, a bitter, pungent plant called selinon, primarily as a medicinal herb and ritual plant rather than a foodstuff — it was used to make garlands for athletes and to treat a variety of ailments, and was strongly associated with death and the underworld in Greek mythology. The cultivated form with the familiar thick, mild stalks was developed in Italy and France during the seventeenth century through selective breeding, and became fashionable on aristocratic tables across Europe by the eighteenth century, when it was expensive enough to be served in special celery glasses as a dinner centerpiece. Celery seed, which carries a far more intense and complex flavor than the stalk, has been used as a spice since ancient times across the Mediterranean and Middle East, and gives celery salt — a fundamental seasoning of American hot dog and burger culture — its distinctive savory, slightly bitter, aromatic character.

Celery's role in American burger and diner culture is perhaps most visible through celery salt, the seasoning blend of ground celery seed and salt that is canonical on the Chicago-style hot dog and that appears in countless burger seasoning blends as a background note of savory complexity. But fresh celery as a burger component has a quieter history, appearing most often in the form of celery-based slaws and relishes in Southern and Midwestern cooking, where the vegetable's clean crunch provides textural contrast and a slightly bitter brightness that cuts through rich beef fat. Paired with bone marrow on this burger, celery plays a specific and crucial role: its clean, slightly herbal freshness and its snap cut through the deep, unctuous richness of the roasted marrow, performing the same function as the parsley and capers in traditional French marrow preparations. The combination is ancient and modern at the same time.

Celery has spent its entire life in my kitchen as the vegetable I bought for one recipe and then left in the refrigerator until it went limp and bitter in the crisper drawer. For years I considered it a supporting character at best — fine in a mirepoix, useful in broth, fundamentally unexciting on its own. What changed my mind was a braised short rib dish I made on a cold February Sunday, where I added celery stalks to the braise and pulled one out near the end to taste it. It had collapsed into silky softness, absorbed the braising liquid, lost its bitterness, and become something deeply savory and aromatic. I started treating celery as a real ingredient after that day. Thinly sliced raw over bone marrow on a burger, it provides what I can only describe as clarity — a cool, clean crunch in the middle of something very rich that makes you want to keep eating.

Medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — is the temperature of a burger patty that has earned its toppings. This burger asks a great deal of the patty: it must support bone marrow, one of the richest substances in any kitchen, and at the same time allow the clean brightness of raw celery to register. That balance is only possible if the patty is juicy, if its fat is rendered but its moisture is retained, if the center is pink and warm and present. The celery's job is to cut through fat and richness; the marrow's job is to double down on richness; the medium-rare patty's job is to be the stable, deeply savory center that gives both of those things a reason to exist. Overcook the patty and the whole construction falls apart — the richness wins and the freshness has nothing to balance. Medium rare is the only answer.
ingredients: 1 egg + 1 tbsp water for egg wash
680g ground beef (80/20 chuck blend), freshly ground
4 center-cut beef femur bones, halved lengthwise by your butcher
3 stalks celery, strings removed and shaved paper-thin on a mandoline or with a vegetable peeler
celery leaves from the inner stalks (pale yellow-green), reserved
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, sugar, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy.
2. Add egg and softened butter. Mix briefly. Add bread flour and salt. Knead with dough hook on medium speed for 8 minutes until smooth.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.
4. Divide into 4 portions (~150g each), shape into tight rounds, place on parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 450°F (230°C). Brush buns with egg wash and sprinkle sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack. Keep oven hot for marrow.

6. Roast the bone marrow: Place bone halves cut-side up on a foil-lined baking sheet. Season with flaky salt and pepper. Roast at 450°F for 15 to 20 minutes until marrow is bubbling and beginning to pull from the bone. Remove, let cool slightly, and scoop out marrow with a small spoon. Keep warm.

7. Prepare the shaved celery: Using a mandoline or vegetable peeler, shave celery stalks into paper-thin ribbons. Place in a bowl of ice water for 5 minutes to crisp. Drain and pat dry. Toss with lemon juice, olive oil, flaky salt, and pepper. Add celery leaves. Set aside.
8. Make the celery-horseradish mayo: Whisk together mayonnaise, horseradish, celery salt, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, and black pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

9. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (170g each). Form into 3/4-inch thick patties with a center dimple. Season both sides with kosher salt, black pepper, celery salt, and garlic powder immediately before cooking.
10. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil.
11. Place patties in the pan. Cook 2 minutes undisturbed. Flip once. Top each patty with a slice of aged white cheddar immediately.
12. Cook 1.5 to 2 minutes more, tenting loosely with foil, until an instant-read thermometer reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack 3 minutes.
13. Toast the buns: Butter cut sides and toast face-down in a skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.
14. Assemble: Spread celery-horseradish mayo on both cut faces of each bun.
15. Layer tomato slices and red onion on the bottom bun. Set the medium-rare cheddar-topped patty on top.

16. Spoon a generous tablespoon of roasted bone marrow over the patty, letting it melt slightly into the cheese. Pile the dressed shaved celery and celery leaves on top of the marrow. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt.
17. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
